articles.title: Zhu Rongji, who helped turn China into a trading giant, dies at 97
articles.summary: The former premier brought China into the WTO and championed reforms that fuelled growth.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Boston Herald via Getty Images By Laura Bicker ,  China correspondent ,  Reporting from Beijing   and   Chen Yan ,  BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Hong Kong 
- Published 12 August 2026 
Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, who spearheaded China's entry into global trade and laid the foundation for its explosive growth, has died at the age of 97. 
He served in the country's second-highest office from 1998-2003 and played a leading role in securing its entry into the World Trade Organization, opening Chinese factories to the international market and drawing foreign investment. 
He was one of the most important economic reformers who moved local tax powers to the central government, closed or privatised failing state firms and promoted home ownership. 
Many in China remember him as a tough and pragmatic leader who delivered double-digit growth and was rarely afraid to speak his mind. 
In 1998, he said China was facing "many potential crises that could erupt at any time... 
"Ordinary people are discontent about us in many ways. Especially, there is corruption among officials, the gulf between rich and poor and the way some local officials act like tyrants." 
He labelled rogue bankers as "half-wits" and said the dams and flood dykes lining the Yangtze River were as "flimsy and porous as tofu dregs". 
Under his leadership, which helped stabilise the economy and tackle corruption, China began transforming into a manufacturing powerhouse, leaving behind its status as a Communist outsider. 
Though he faced criticism because those reforms also led to 30 million lay-offs over five years, and with huge growth came more inequality. 
Chinese state media describe Zhu Rongji's life as one of "revolution, struggle and brilliance". 
He was born in the central province of Hunan in 1928 and earned a degree in electrical engineering before joining the civil service. 
He joined the Communist Party in 1949, but was purged twice - first after criticising Mao Zedong's economic policies as "irrational" and being labelled a "rightist", and again during the Cultural Revolution. 
Zhu was brought back into the fold after Mao's death, and by 1991 had risen to the role of vice-premier in charge of China's economy. 
He took the role of premier seven years later. 
Image source, Boston Herald via Getty Images Image caption, 
Zhu Rongji was a keen opponent of official corruption 
Zhu led China through difficult negotiations to enter the World Trade Organization in 2002. 
In state media his obituary described him as an "outstanding member of the Communist Party of China and loyal Commnist fighter... an outstanding leader of the Party and state".

articles.title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
articles.summary: "Flash marriage" scams are an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis long in the making in China.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scams By Laura Bicker China correspondent ,  Reporting from Beijing and Guiyang 
- Published 10 August 2026 
At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts. 
They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman. 
"The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you." 
So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate. 
He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married. 
Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over. 
"My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head. 
He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie. 
She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age. 
He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches. 
"My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalance 
Wang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China. 
For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance. 
There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia. 
This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand. 
"The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says. 
Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden. 
Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages". 
Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older. 
So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which had "bred illegal practices and chaos". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radar 
It's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry. 
This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern". 
In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000). 
"I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC. 
Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub. 
The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles. 
Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud. 
So he paid up and the introductions began. 
Image caption, 
Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse 
He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids. 
He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him. 
"She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest." 
They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined. 
After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it. 
"If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan." 
The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. 
In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background. 
Image caption, 
Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding 
Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money. 
Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents. 
When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price. 
He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared. 
From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong. 
In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave. 
Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived. 
"There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us. 
The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC. 
They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them. 
"Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with." 
One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating". 
Image caption, 
It was in a room like this where Wang met his bride 
Wang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels. 
His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage. 
On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag. 
He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency. 
Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room. 
Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims. 
"All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed." 
But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced. 
He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses. 
Image caption, 
The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeks 
The agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients. 
"The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well." 
They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential". 
He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back. 
"I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed. 
"We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible." 
Image caption, 
This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuine 
This brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved. 
"I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says. 
He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages." 
He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime. 
These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many. 
For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money. 
"In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says. 
"In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove." 
Image caption, 
Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed men 
Even harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash. 
Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all. 
"After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now." 
Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo. 
"It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork. 
"I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

articles.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
articles.summary: Typhoon Dolphin has made landfall, bringing strong winds and heavy rain across eastern China including Shanghai.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Lorry overturns as typhoon hits China By Kelly Ng 
- Published 10 August 2026 
Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall. 
The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday. 
While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north. 
Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year. 
It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said. 
Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in eastern China on Sunday evening 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Residents wade through flooded streets in Shanghai 
Governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai. 
Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai, an area popular with tourists, and people wading through ankle-deep waters. 
Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties. 
Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say. 
Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters. 
Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou. 
In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects. 
The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. 
It also has a massive circulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The typhoon has disrupted transportation services 
Misinformation around the storm has apparently spread rapidly on the Chinese internet, with state media reporting that two people have been detained for distributing such content. 
One of them, a 60-year-old man, created a fake video with AI that claimed someone in Shanghai had fallen from a building during the storm. 
Another man, 32, had re-edited storm footage posted by other social media users in a way that was deemed as misleading. 
Dolphin brought torrential rains to the Philippines, parts of northern Taiwan and Japan's Okinawa island before bearing down on China. 
- 
AI or real? BBC analyses viral China disaster videos 
- Published 5 August 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide in the Philippines 
Eight people have died in the Philippines because of heavy monsoon rains brought on by Dolphin and storms earlier in the week, says the Office of Civil Defence. More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide. 
In Okinawa in Japan, five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the prefectural government. 
Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. 
Meanwhile in Hong Kong, weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as the typhoon swept warm air over the city. 
Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. 
This year is a strong El Niño year, which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense.

articles.title: 'I lost $14,000 in a month': Investors hit by Korean stock market's wild swings
articles.summary: Some traders are reeling from heavy losses after a brutal correction in South Korea's stock market.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Kim Yongjoon Image caption, 
Yongjoon Kim, pictured with his partner, planned to use his investments to fund a new home as they are getting married later this year By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 37 minutes ago 
Bank worker Yongjoon Kim lost 20 million Korean won ($14,000; £10,500) on the South Korean stock market last month. 
Kim's money was meant to help buy a home, as he is getting married later this year. 
Instead the value of his tech investments slumped by around 25% in July. 
"It's going to sting and I'm going to have to work really hard to make up for this," Kim says. "But for others who have taken more risk, they're going to feel the pain." 
Many of his friends are worse off, and now in a "desperate" situation after "going all in" with their savings, he says. 
While plenty of investors are piling into technology stocks , sharp market swings mean the bets don't always pay off, with prices often moving on every major headline. 
Nowhere is that instability more pronounced than in South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi, widely regarded as the world's most volatile stock index. 
A global frenzy around artificial intelligence has driven wild swings in the value of the country's biggest chipmakers. 
The Kospi faced "one of the sharpest corrections" in its history between June and August, comparable to the drops seen during Covid-19 and the 1997 Asian financial crisis, says Wee Khoon Chong from financial services company BNY. 
The index more than doubled its value since the start of the year to rise above 9,000 points in mid-June, before plunging to 5,500 within a few weeks. It has now recovered some ground to about 6,800 points. 
A key reason for the sell-off in recent weeks has been concerns over the huge amounts of money being spent on AI, Wee adds. 
The slump has had a big impact on many of the country's personal investors who bought tech stocks over the past year. 
For Woongsa Kim, a look at his shares trading app is a painful reminder of what he had made then lost by investing in the South Korean stock market. 
At the start of the year, he used about half of a bonus from work to buy shares in tech giant SK Hynix. 
The stock quadrupled in value before most of those gains were wiped out, leaving his investment, now worth about 300 million won, at roughly half the value of its peak. 
"Thinking about it just brings tears to my eyes," Kim told the BBC. 
Image source, Woongsa Kim Image caption, 
Woongsa Kim put half of a bonus into SK Hynix shares 
The sell-off came after tech shares had soared for months, "generating the extreme euphoria" that has moved some personal investors to take out loans to invest, says investment analyst Tobias Reger. 
It has been most acutely felt by people who used leverage - a form of borrowing in the financial markets. 
Leveraging lets an investor control a larger number of stocks than their own cash would otherwise allow, which delivers a bigger profit if the shares rise. 
However, if the stocks fall past an agreed level it can trigger what is known as a margin call - when a broker demands payment of the debt. 
By the end of July an estimated 1.2 million South Korean personal investor accounts had faced margin calls, equivalent to about one in every 30 working-age adults in the country. 
Leveraged trading is a growing trend among personal investors that has also picked up in markets like Taiwan and the US, says Frank Benzimra, the head of Asia equity strategy at financial services group Societe Generale. 
That has raised the risks around AI-related stocks, he adds. 
'Gut-wrenching' slump 
After his US-listed Nvidia shares soared by more than 1,000%, Chanyong Park, who works in marketing, says he put most of the profits into SK Hynix shares. But that bet went sour as their value has fallen by around $10,000. 
"This was money I'd invested to save before planning to leave my job around October to start my own business. But now I'm seriously wondering whether I'll have enough." 
Park plans to hold on to his SK Hynix shares in hopes of a rebound, although recent swings have made him hesitant to invest more. 
"It doesn't always feel like movements are driven by rational reasons - sometimes it still feels a lot like gambling," he says. 
Another investor Youngji Park says he went "all in", putting the majority of his available cash into Samsung shares that peaked at a total value of 45 million Korean won. 
But his investment has suffered a "gut-wrenching" slump, Park says.

- Published 20 July 
- 
Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m? 
- Published 27 July 
He too plans to keep hold of his shares in the hope that they will rise again. 
"I feel like a fool for trusting the Korean stock market," he says. "It's a long-term game now. I'll just have to wait it out." 
College student Soomin Yi says she pooled money with a friend to invest in SK Hynix after experiencing "fomo" (fear of missing out). 
Image source, Soomin Yi Image caption, 
Soomin Yi says she did not study investing seriously before buying shares 
But she now wishes she had sold her shares in the company when they peaked at three million won each in June, instead of buying into speculation that they would rise to five million won. 
"We didn't really have anyone around us who is experienced in investing, and we did not study investing seriously before buying the stock," Yi says. 
What this means for the rest of the world 
The huge swings in Korean shares are also raising concerns about some other markets around the world. 
Tech-heavy indexes like Japan's Nikkei 225 seem to be moving in tandem with the Kospi's wild swings, Societe Generale's Benzimra says. 
But the majority of the world's stock markets are unlikely to see that level of violent moves as they include a wider mix of companies, he adds. 
"I don't think we can see the same kind of volatility in large diversified markets such as the [Tokyo Stock Price Index] or the US equity markets," Benzimra says. 
And traders who diversified their portfolios say it has helped cushion the blow from the stock market rout. 
"I think this whole episode is a warning to Korean investors, especially young investors, not to put everything in one basket and hope for the best," says Yongjoon Kim, who also has shares in overseas markets. 
He adds that he should have taken a more cautious approach to investing in tech stocks. 
His fiancée, Gaeon Lee, is optimistic that the market will recover despite losing part of the savings they had set aside for a new home. 
But she worries about Kim, saying the constant need to monitor their investments has taken a toll on him. 
"Seeing our home savings take a hit in the stock market was definitely a wake-up call," she says.

articles.title: Japan PM says Putin's visit to disputed islands 'absolutely unacceptable'
articles.summary: It was the first time the Russian leader had visited the Kuril islands, according to state media.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Russia's President Vladimir Putin tastes caviar as he visits Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu By Koh Ewe   and   Kurumi Mori ,  Tokyo correspondent 
- Published 13 August 2026, 05:46 BST Updated 10:54 BST 
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has criticised Vladimir Putin's first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril islands on Thursday as "absolutely unacceptable". 
Russian state media reported that Putin visited Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, one of four islands in the Kuril chain that are claimed by Russia and Japan. 
Putin's trip "has worsened Japanese sentiment towards Russia," Takaichi told reporters, maintaining the island chain was "a unique territory of [Japan] historically and under international law". 
The countries have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. 
The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. Four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. 
They are administered by Russia. At the end of World War Two, the Soviet Union annexed the island chain and deported around 17,000 Japanese residents. 
During his visit, Putin sampled fish roe and spoke to island locals, Russian state media reported. 
Speaking from the prime minister's office on Thursday, Takaichi said his trip "wounds the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories". 
"I hope that the Russian side will take the gravity of this matter very seriously," she said. 
Earlier that day, Japan's foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi said the islands were "inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit". 
Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. 
Japan has protested against previous visits by Russian officials to the disputed islands, including Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his predecessor Dmitry Medvedev. 
The Kuril islands are a strategic area for Russia, which has beefed up its military presence on the islands over the past decade. The island of Iturup is used as its primary military air base in the region. 
Last month, Chinese and Russian naval warships sailed through a strait in the Kuril islands during a joint patrol. 
Russia also holds regular military drills near the islands, drawing condemnation from Japan.

articles.title: BTS star V reveals hearing loss battle during livestream
articles.summary: The K-pop star says he has suffered hearing issues for over two years before revealing it publicly this week.
articles.full_text:
Image source, MLB Photos via Getty Images Image caption, 
BTS member V says he has been dealing with hearing issues for more than two years By Koh Ewe 
- Published 13 August 2026, 05:09 BST 
V, a member of pop sensation BTS, says he has been receiving treatment for hearing loss in one ear, an announcement that comes midway through the band's highly-anticipated world tour. 
In a livestream on Wednesday, the 30-year-old said that he has dealt with the problem for about two and a half years. This was the first time he was revealing it to the band's fans, he said. 
"If the hearing in my left ear is at 100, it's only about 30 in my right," said V, whose real name is Kim Tae-hyung. 
The band is currently on its first world tour in years, marking the reunion of all seven members since they went on a hiatus for mandatory military service. 
During the livestream, V said his hearing became worse when he was serving in the military. 
But he said he did not take it seriously at first, believing it to be "a matter of mental strength". 
He added he was now taking medication and going to hospital regularly. 
With rare exceptions, all able-bodied men are required to serve 18 months of military service in South Korea. 
This included BTS members, who were at the height of their fame in 2022 when they started taking career breaks to enlist in the military. 
V joined the military in 2023 and was discharged in June 2025. 
The Arirang World Tour, which kicked off in April in South Korea, marked the highly-anticipated reunion of the band's seven members. 
The livestream on Wednesday came after the band wrapped its concerts in Baltimore, Maryland. 
V was joined by his bandmate Jungkook, who talked about a shin injury he has been dealing with during the tour, saying he was "on the verge of developing a stress fracture". 
Jungkook added that he would have to manage his injury well in order to keep performing. 
In the coming months, the concert tour will take BTS to cities around the world, including Los Angeles, Buenos Aires, Bangkok, Sydney and Hong Kong.

articles.title: South Korea's Incheon airport becomes world's busiest for global traffic
articles.summary: The airport said diversions caused by the Middle East conflict helped boost its traffic, while Heathrow was ranked second.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Incheon International Airport is the main gateway to South Korea By Kelly Ng 
- Published 13 August 2026, 06:49 BST 
South Korea's Incheon has become the world's busiest airport by international passenger traffic for the first time, new figures show. 
Incheon International Airport, the main gateway to South Korea, served 38.4 million international passengers for the first six months of this year, according to preliminary data from the Airports Council International. 
London Heathrow Airport ranked second with 37.79 million passengers, followed by Singapore's Changi Airport with 34.53 million. 
Incheon's airport attributed its rise partly to the diversion of passengers from aviation hubs in the Middle East because of the conflict between the US and Iran. 
Dubai International Airport, which ranked second both in 2024 and 2025 based on full-year statistics, is expected to fall outside the top five this time. 
London's Heathrow airport ranked fifth in 2024 and seventh in 2025, while Incheon ranked 12th and 13th, respectively. 
Some passengers who previously transited through Dubai on the way to Europe are now travelling via Incheon, the airport corporation said, fuelling an 18% rise in transfer passengers from the same period last year. 
The number of transfer passengers whose final destinations were in Europe rose 63.2% to 210,000, it added. 
The corporation said the expansion of infrastructure also enabled the airport to manage a larger traffic load. Incheon, which opened in 2001, serves 158 international destinations. 
In comparison, Hong Kong's International Airport serves 139 destinations, Shanghai's Pudong serves 92 while Tokyo's Narita serves 86. 
"We're grateful for the [South Korean] government's support, the public's encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport in making Incheon the world's No. 1 airport," said the Incheon airport corporation's acting president Kim Beom-ho. 
Kim added the corporation planned to strengthen competitiveness by focusing on passenger convenience.

articles.title: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
articles.summary: Malaysia's Forest City was pitched as "paradise" but last month police raided it over alleged scam operations.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Scammers busted in Southeast Asia's biggest ghost town By Gavin Butler Reporting from Forest City, Malaysia 
- Published 12 August 2026 
From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline. 
When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that. 
Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust. 
"In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties. 
"If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better." 
As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract. 
In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people ‌and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems. 
From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police. 
Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations. 
The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response. 
Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg – and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising. 
Image source, BBC/ Gavin Butler Image caption, 
Forest City was meant to house some 700,000 residents - but the current population is thought to be less than 1% of that 
"The reality is that many of these organisations now resemble multinational corporations more than a traditional organised crime network or gang," says John Wojcik, an analyst at TRM Labs, which investigates crypto-facilitated crime. "They have dedicated recruitment teams, IT departments, money-laundering specialists and infrastructure." 
Authorities and experts agree that the Forest City operations were probably staffed by criminals who had been driven out of Cambodia, a global nerve centre for transnational scams. 
Over the past five years, this criminal sector has ballooned into a multi-billion-dollar industry, built on the forced labour of brutalised trafficking victims who work under threat of torture and abuse. 
Since late last year, the Cambodian government has stepped up efforts to stamp out these operations. Authorities recently estimated that 300,000 people had left the country within a few months as raids on industrial-scale compounds intensified. 
But these Malaysian offshoots do not appear to have been scam "compounds" in the traditional sense. 
Compared to more infamous walled complexes in places like Sihanoukville or the Myanmar borderlands, the alleged scam hubs in Forest City appear almost white collar, reportedly staffed by local residents and sitting wall-to-wall with the homes of unsuspecting neighbours. 
Image source, BBC/ Gavin Butler Image caption, 
Forest City's sales gallery features a gigantic diorama of the complex in miniature 
Kevin, a tenant who also works in property sales for Forest City, believes scammers are still operating in "condominiums or serviced apartments" in the complex. He asked for his name to be changed for fear of repercussions. 
"We know what they're doing," he says. "This is actually a very common issue in Johor city and Kuala Lumpur, but especially in Forest City. Forest City is very special." 
Part of what makes Forest City "special", according to Kevin, Wojcik and others, is the very thing that has gained it so much notoriety: its reputation as a semi-abandoned "ghost city". 
"When we speak to clients or customers, the company teaches us to say 'we already have 23,000 residents living in this area'," says Kevin – but the reality, he quietly adds, is there are "less than 5,000". 
"That's the reason" scammers have chosen Forest City to set up shop, he suggests. 
"They have their own privacy... Nobody comes here." 
Image source, BBC/ Gavin Butler Image caption, 
Shuttered buildings and dilapidated infrastructure are a common sight in Forest City 
There are several factors which precipitated what many see as the downfall of Forest City. 
Spearheaded by Country Garden, one of China's largest property developers, and Danga 88, a private company controlled by Malaysian Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, the project was initially dreamed up as an eco-friendly metropolis for well-heeled Chinese clients - featuring a high-end hotel, golf course and water park. The resort-style city's seafront offices and apartments were expected to be in high demand. 
But the combined weight of the Covid pandemic, China's spiralling property slump and constricted borrowing limits for its citizens have sunk those sky-high ambitions, and all but ground the project to a standstill. 
The lights are still on, but almost no-one is home. 
And that appears to have made the complex a honeypot for scammers. 
"Forest City reflects the conditions organised crime have been targeting for years - a flagship location marketed as a prestigious, luxury, master-planned smart city that never came close to fulfilling that vision," Wojcik says. 
"Developments like this offer precisely what these syndicates look for: modern infrastructure, large numbers of vacant properties, and international connectivity all wrapped around the veneer of legitimate economic activity to ensure that the criminal nature of what goes on inside remains unnoticed." 
With this in mind, the glittering facade of Forest City echoes a more infamous metropolis 1,800 kilometres (1,120 miles) to the north: Shwe Kokko, the so-called resort city on Myanmar's Thai border, which is one of the world's most notorious scam hubs. 
Built by the private Chinese conglomerate Yatai, Shwe Kokko markets itself as a safe holiday destination for Chinese tourists and a haven for the super-rich. But behind its tree-lined streets and luxury villas is a nexus of fraud, money-laundering and human trafficking. 
Image source, BBC/ Gavin Butler Image caption, 
The complex sits on Malaysia's southernmost tip, less than five kilometres (three miles) from Singapore 
For all its headwinds, and despite the fact that only 15 to 20% of the originally proposed project has been completed, Forest City similarly still markets itself as an up-and-coming hotbed for property investment, tech innovation and tax-free business ventures. 
Such entrepreneurial packaging serves as a Trojan horse for scammers wanting to set up shop without drawing unwanted attention – and allows them to perpetrate their fraud more effectively. 
Wojcik explains that "when scam syndicates can embed themselves behind seemingly legitimate businesses in ordinary commercial developments, they not only become more difficult to detect and disrupt, they become capable of exerting serious amounts of power and influence through the massive profits they generate". 
This power and influence in turn allows scammers to professionalise in other ways. 
Though human trafficking still largely fuels much of the scam industry's labour force, there is now a noticeable trend of syndicate operators recruiting and retaining experienced scammers with higher pay and better working conditions. 
Meanwhile, in the same Telegram groups where scam jobs are being advertised, career scammers are also now posting detailed resumes, outlining their experience in fraudulent activities and emphasising their eagerness to work. 
"It's a sign the industry is maturing into a more professionalised criminal enterprise," Wojcik explains, "while coercion and exploitation still remain widespread". 
The Forest City raids highlight a transnational scam industry that is shifting in size and shape. But this is far from the first time such operations have been detected in Malaysia. 
Throughout 2022, before the industry gained widespread global attention, Malaysian authorities raided several scam centres operating out of bungalows and condominiums in the southern state of Johor, the northern state of Penang and the capital city of Kuala Lumpur. 
Yet while these and other major crackdowns sent a message of zero tolerance to fraud syndicates, Wojcik notes that Malaysia has remained home to influential criminal networks - and that "any signs of large-scale re-emergence deserve close attention". 
Image source, BBC/ Gavin Butler Image caption, 
The $100-billion dollar complex's quiet streets and deserted beaches have earned it a reputation as a "ghost city" 
In Forest City, such signs may already be emerging. 
Kevin says it's long been an "open secret" that scams are happening here, and that "the only shocking thing is that the police were effective". 
He's certain there are more, too – but is unperturbed at the idea that his neighbours might be defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars. 
"For me, I don't care," he says. "It's not my business... I work here just for the salary." 
Other residents feel the same way. 
Phillip, whose name we have also changed, moved to Forest City from Singapore last year, attracted by the relatively cheap property market and the idea that he could get more value for his money. He works in tech, and says he is "very focused" on the topic of cyber protection. 
"Yes they [the scammers] might be on my doorstep, they might be my neighbours... [they] could be one of the ones that's running one of these syndicates. At the end of the day, it doesn't matter where you go – this is going to happen." 
He says he was "not surprised" to hear about the reports of scam centres in his complex. What has surprised him is the fact that "more and more people are moving" to Forest City. 
One of the reasons he chose the development where he lives is because of the peace and quiet, he says – but he's pleased to see that it is evolving from a "ghost town" into a place where people seem to want to be. 
"So many people have lost money on these developments," he points out. "But the last three months, you see the lights on in the condos. You've gone from one in 20 to maybe one in five."

articles.title: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft
articles.summary: A 97-year-old's dramatic rescue captures how Assam's floods are reaching places once thought safe.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar By Soutik Biswas 
India correspondent 
- Published 12 August 2026 
Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother. 
Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety. 
"Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says. 
An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts. 
The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves. 
By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it. 
Image caption, 
Baruah quit journalism to concentrate on animal husbandry 
The scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam. 
The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps. 
The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated. 
For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound. 
"This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says. 
Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime. 
Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km. 
Image caption, 
A 97-year-old Lokada Duarah was carried onto a banana tree trunk and taken to safety after floodwaters rose around her home 
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, 
A boy uses a makeshift banana raft to navigate floodwaters in Assam 
She had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building. 
Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'. 
Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it. 
She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed. 
None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says. 
The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly. 
Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages. 
About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp. 
Image caption, 
Baruah and her family abandoned their home nearly a day after the water began rising 
For five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil. 
Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats. Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill. 
But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before? 
Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley, a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms". 
The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A family shelters inside a tent in Sivasagar district, among more than 5,000 people lodged in 252 relief camps 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Amit Giri holds a photo of his father, Siv Sankar Giri, who died in the floods, outside their damaged home in Sivasagar. He is among 100 people killed in the floods. 
As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251. 
In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat. 
Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology. 
Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam. 
"What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography. 
For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal. 
Image caption, 
Only 60 of Baruah's goats survived the floods 
She has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week. 
Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have. 
So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life. 
She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance. 
Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee? 
"No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before." 
"We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."
